title: Walking Is Not Enough. A New Study Says Vigorous Exercise and Sleep Are What Actually Protect Your Mental Health.
excerpt: A University of Oulu study of middle-aged adults found that moderate-to-vigorous physical activity and adequate sleep dramatically reduced symptoms of depression and anxiety — and light walking barely moved the needle.
body:
For years, the standard advice has been simple: move more. Take a walk after dinner. Get your steps in. Doctors say it, wellness influencers repeat it, and health apps buzz at you until you do it.

A new study from the University of Oulu in Finland, published in the journal *Depression and Anxiety*, argues that this advice is incomplete — and possibly misleading. The researchers found that moderate-to-vigorous physical activity and adequate sleep are the two factors that actually protect mental health in middle-aged adults. Light physical activity, including the kind of leisurely walking most people default to, produced limited benefits.

## The Study That Changes the Conversation

The Finnish researchers tracked physical activity patterns, sleep duration, and mental health outcomes in a cohort of middle-aged adults. They used accelerometer data rather than self-reported activity levels, which makes the findings more reliable than many previous studies.

The results were unambiguous. The more time participants spent in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity — the kind that leaves you slightly out of breath — the fewer symptoms of depression and anxiety they reported. Replacing sedentary time with light activity produced some benefit, but the effect was small and inconsistent across different symptom measures.

"The findings suggest that, from a mental health perspective, the intensity of physical activity is key, not merely increasing movement as such," said Maisa Niemelä, an adjunct professor at the University of Oulu.

Sleep emerged as the other critical variable. Participants who got sufficient sleep showed consistently better mental health outcomes, regardless of their activity levels. The study suggests that the daily balance between vigorous exercise, adequate sleep, and time spent sedentary matters more than any single behaviour in isolation.

## Why South Asians Need to Pay Closer Attention

South Asians in the diaspora face a particular version of this problem. The community's default relationship with exercise tends to favour low-intensity activity — evening walks after dinner, gentle yoga, morning strolls in the neighbourhood. These are culturally embedded habits, and they are not bad. But this study suggests they may not be sufficient to protect against the mental health challenges that disproportionately affect immigrant communities.

Research consistently shows that South Asian immigrants in the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada report higher rates of anxiety and depression than the general population. The stressors are well-documented: immigration-related isolation, cultural dislocation, caregiving pressures for elderly parents back home, and the relentless performance expectations that come with being part of a high-achieving diaspora.

The American Heart Association has previously noted that South Asians in the US are among the least physically active ethnic groups, with lower rates of vigorous exercise than non-Hispanic white, Black, and Hispanic adults. A 2024 study in the MASALA cohort — the largest longitudinal study of South Asian Americans — found that only 38 per cent of participants met the recommended 150 minutes per week of moderate-to-vigorous activity.

## What Counts as Vigorous Enough

The threshold is lower than most people assume. Moderate-to-vigorous activity includes brisk walking at a pace fast enough to make conversation slightly difficult, cycling, swimming, jogging, dancing, playing badminton or cricket, or even vigorous housework like scrubbing floors or carrying heavy groceries up stairs.

The key distinction is between movement that elevates your heart rate and breathing, and movement that does not. A slow evening walk through the park is pleasant and social. It is not, according to this research, doing much for your mental health.

## The Sleep Factor

The study's emphasis on sleep carries particular weight for the South Asian diaspora. Oura ring data, Fitbit studies, and sleep surveys consistently show that South Asian adults in the US sleep less than the recommended seven to nine hours per night. Cultural factors play a role — late dinners, evening socialising, long work hours in demanding professions, and the habit of staying connected with family across time zones all compress sleep windows.

The Finnish study found that insufficient sleep eroded mental health gains even among participants who exercised vigorously. The implication is that a punishing 5 AM gym routine followed by five hours of sleep is not a winning strategy.

## What This Means for You

The prescription that emerges from this research is not complicated, but it requires honesty about current habits. If your primary form of exercise is walking, consider adding two to three sessions per week of something that makes you breathe hard — a fast-paced badminton game, a cycling session, a group fitness class, or even running intervals in your neighbourhood.

And protect your sleep. Not as an afterthought, but as a non-negotiable component of your mental health infrastructure. The Oulu study makes clear that exercise and sleep are not separate health goals. They are interlocking systems, and neglecting either one undermines the other.

The evening walk is not the enemy. But if it is all you are doing, it may not be enough.
